raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old previously healthy male was admitted to our medical unit with a history of fever of 5-day duration. He had high-grade fever associated with generalized aches and frontal headache. He denied any respiratory or urinary symptoms. He mentioned that he had not passed faeces for the last three days but had developed nonbloody diarrhoea on the day of admission without any vomiting or abdominal pain. He denied any recent travel, but he had been eating from various food outlets for the past 2 weeks during his after-school cricket practice sessions.
On examination, he was not ill looking despite his temperature of 40 C. There were no pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, and skin rashes. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, nontender abdomen with a 3 cm nontender hepatomegaly and a 2 cm splenomegaly. His blood test showed a haemoglobin count of 14.8 g/dl, a white cell count of 2.8 x 109/l (neutrophils 79% and lymphocytes 14%), and a platelet count of 97 x 109/l. Dengue NS1 antigen and IgM against dengue virus detected by a commercial kit (Standard Diagnostics, Inc., Germany) were negative. C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated more than 250 mg/dl in two subsequent samples. His liver function tests were normal except elevated liver transaminases (ALT 145 U/l and AST 118 U/l; ALT/AST normal range 8-40 U/L). An ultrasound scan of the abdomen confirmed mild hepatosplenomegaly. On days 2 and 3 of his admission, he continued to have high fever spikes, diarrhoea, and persistent thrombocytopenia with a high CRP.
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily was commenced. After 48 hours, the patients' clinical condition had not improved and the high fever spikes continued. After antibiotic susceptibility test results, his antibiotic was changed to imipenem 1 g 8 hourly. He showed clinical improvement after 48 hours, but the diarrhoea and fever settled only around the 10th day of treatment. Imipenem was continued for a total duration of 14 days. His platelet count, liver transaminases, and CRP returned to normal. A repeat blood and faeces culture performed on discharge was negative for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old previously healthy male presented with fever of 5 days duration associated with generalized body aches and frontal headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: High-grade fever began 5 days prior to admission, accompanied by generalized body aches and frontal headache. He experienced constipation for 3 days, followed by the onset of nonbloody diarrhea on the day of admission. He denied vomiting, abdominal pain, or respiratory and urinary symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Denied recent travel. Epidemiological exposure: had consumed food from various local outlets over the past 2 weeks during after-school cricket practice sessions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denied vomiting, abdominal pain, respiratory symptoms, or urinary symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Not ill-looking despite temperature of 40 °C. No pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, or skin rashes. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations normal. Abdomen was soft and nontender, with 3 cm nontender hepatomegaly and 2 cm splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 14.8 g/dL; white cell count: 2.8 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 79%, lymphocytes 14%); platelet count: 97 x 10^9/L. Dengue NS1 antigen and IgM against dengue virus: negative. CRP: elevated >250 mg/dL in two subsequent samples. Liver function tests: ALT 145 U/L, AST 118 U/L (normal range 8-40 U/L); other liver function tests normal. Abdominal ultrasound: confirmed mild hepatosplenomegaly.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever due to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. The patient was initially treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily, but remained febrile with diarrhea and persistent thrombocytopenia after 48 hours. Following antibiotic susceptibility results demonstrating resistance, antibiotic therapy was switched to intravenous imipenem 1 g every 8 hours. Clinical improvement was observed within 48 hours; fever and diarrhea resolved around day 10 of treatment. Imipenem was continued for a total duration of 14 days, with complete normalization of platelet count, liver transaminases, and CRP. Repeat blood and feces cultures performed at discharge were negative for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
